findings.title: Unchecked nil dereference of device config
findings.message: The inspector dereferences `p.Device.Current` and `p.Device.Load` without a nil check. If a component has a current-device kind but its config pointer is nil, rendering the inspector panics. That could happen with a legacy or partially loaded project, or a snapshot taken mid-update. The defaults were already computed, so falling back to them or skipping the controls is cheap.
findings.suggestion: Guard the dereferences. Either fall back to the defaults or return nil when the config pointer is nil.

findings.title: Possible nil map write panic on missing schema property
findings.message: `inputProperty` can return nil, which is why the local `bounds` helper checks for it. These two lines index the result directly: `inputProperty(schema, "version")` and `inputProperty(schema, "mode")`. If the property is missing, the write is to a nil map. That panics during schema construction, e.g. when the field is renamed or `kind` is passed incorrectly.

findings.title: Unguarded nil map write for load mode enum
findings.message: This is the same unguarded `inputProperty` result as on line 148. If the `mode` property is absent from the load schema, assigning to the nil map panics.
findings.suggestion: Nil-check the returned map before assigning `enum`.

findings.title: Current source can be selected as primary voltage supply
findings.message: `current-source` is now added to `sources`, so it can be `sources[0]` and become the primary source. `out.Supply` then becomes the current source's positive net, and `out.Circuit = Circuit{out.Source.Value, ...}` reads a current in amps as a supply voltage. This can produce a wrong supply/output net and wrong legacy circuit values when the circuit also has a battery or DC source.
findings.suggestion: When choosing `out.Source`, prefer voltage sources over `current-source`. Fall back to the current source only when no voltage source exists, and handle that case explicitly in the `Circuit` construction.

findings.title: Possible nil dereference of Device.Load
findings.message: `p.Device.Load.Mode` is read with no nil check. If `Device` or `Load` is a pointer that can be unset, for example on a freshly placed load or on a malformed graph, building annotations panics while the service lock is held.
findings.suggestion: Check for nil before the read: `p.Device != nil && p.Device.Load != nil && p.Device.Load.Mode == "cp"`. Better still, read the mode through the same accessor that `currentWaveform` uses.

findings.title: Corner/step logic uses p.Pulse while annotations use currentWaveform
findings.message: The annotations get a current device's pulse from `currentWaveform(p)`, but the step and corner logic reads `p.Pulse` directly. If current-device pulses are stored somewhere other than `p.Pulse`, edge corners and step limits are skipped. The integrator could then step over the current pulse transitions.
findings.suggestion: Get the pulse from the same place everywhere. For example, use `currentWaveform(p).Pulse` for current devices in `nextSourceCorner` and `maximumWaveformStep`, or check that `currentWaveform` always returns `p.Pulse`.
findings.evidence: next = math.Min(next, nextSourceCorner(p, t, at, p.ID == n.c.Source.ID && !IsCurrentDevice(p.Kind)))

findings.title: Closure captures loop variable f
findings.message: The setter closure captures the range variable `f`. If the module targets a Go version before 1.22, every timing field would call the last entry's setter, so every field would edit the fall time.
findings.suggestion: Shadow the loop variable (`f := f`) before creating the closure, or confirm go.mod targets Go 1.22 or later.
findings.evidence: field(f.id, f.label, f.value*1000, .001, 10000, .1, func(v float64) { t := timing; f.set(&t, decimalControlSI(v, -3)); setTiming(t) })

fix.before: field(f.id, f.label, f.value*1000, .001, 10000, .1, func(v float64) { t := timing; f.set(&t, decimalControlSI(v, -3)); setTiming(t) })
fix.after:
f := f
			field(f.id, f.label, f.value*1000, .001, 10000, .1, func(v float64) { t := timing; f.set(&t, decimalControlSI(v, -3)); setTiming(t) })

findings.title: Model description appended as a Fact instead of Limitations
findings.message: Every other case that applies a model-level description puts it in `out.Model`/`out.Limitations`, as the passive-loss branches do. Here the long model ID and limitations text is appended to `Facts` instead. Facts are meant to describe this component in the current circuit. The result is a duplicated, misclassified paragraph in the explanation. `Model` and `Limitations` may also stay at whatever `part.Model`/`partLimitations` produced.
findings.suggestion: Set `out.Model, out.Limitations = CurrentDeviceModelID, currentDeviceDescription` and only append `currentDeviceName(part)` to Facts.

fix.after:
case "current-source", "electronic-load":
		out.Model, out.Limitations = CurrentDeviceModelID, currentDeviceDescription
		out.Facts = append(out.Facts, currentDeviceName(part))

findings.title: Hard current clamp creates non-smooth Jacobian
findings.message: The current source uses `smoothLevel` so Newton iterations see a continuous derivative. The load's maximum-current limit is a hard clamp, so the derivative jumps from a positive value to 0 at the limit. The CP linear-region boundary at MinimumVoltage also has a slope discontinuity, from level/Vmin² to -level/Vmin². These kinks can make Newton oscillate across the boundary and slow or break convergence in transient steps.
findings.suggestion: Use a smooth limiter, for example the same `smoothLevel` helper or a soft-min, so the current and its derivative are continuous at the limit.

findings.title: Initial readout assertion can pass vacuously
findings.message: The initial-readout assertion only runs when `state.Transient` is non-nil. If a regression leaves `Transient` nil, the check is skipped silently and the test passes without verifying the initial voltage trace.
findings.suggestion: Assert that `state.Transient` is non-nil first, or fail when it is nil, before comparing the values.

findings.title: Redundant current-device dispatch in waveformComponents
findings.message: `withDeviceWaveform` already returns `currentWaveform(p)` for current devices. The extra if/else in `waveformComponents` repeats that dispatch, so the two code paths can drift apart if one is changed later.
findings.suggestion: Remove the branch and always call `withDeviceWaveform(p)`.

findings.title: Test bumps command count without asserting the new commands
findings.message: The test raises the expected command count from 30 to 32 but never checks that `current-source.configure` and `load.configure` are the two commands that were added. Any two unrelated commands would make it pass.

findings.title: Dead x-model-id assignment overwritten after switch
findings.message: The new case sets `schema["x-model-id"]` inside the switch. After the switch, `schema["x-model-id"] = ExtendedModelID` unconditionally overwrites it, and the new `if` then restores it. The in-switch assignment has no effect. This is misleading: a later edit to the post-switch block could silently change the model ID.
findings.suggestion: Remove the dead assignment inside the case. Better, compute the model ID in each case and assign it once after the switch, instead of chaining `if id == ...` overrides.

findings.title: No cutset validation for ideal current sources
findings.message: Current sources are skipped in the grounding check, the ideal-capacitor check and the constraint union-find. However, there is no check for topologies that are ill-posed for an ideal current source. Examples are a current source with an open circuit or a cutset made only of current sources and inductors, such as two current sources in series. These topologies have an indeterminate node voltage or KCL inconsistency. Voltage-source loops are rejected explicitly, but the dual cutset case is not.
findings.suggestion: Add a dual check that rejects networks where a current source forms a cutset with only other current sources or inductors. Alternatively, require a resistive or conductive path in parallel or series as appropriate, and fail with an `ideal-constraint-cutset` diagnostic.
findings.evidence: if v.Kind != "current-source" && v.Kind != "battery" && v.Kind != "dc-source" && net(v, "negative") != out.Ground {

findings.title: Electronic-load unit only handles cp mode
findings.message: The unit is "A" for every load mode except constant power. Loads usually also have constant-resistance (Ω) and constant-voltage (V) modes. If this load supports them, the pulse annotation shows the wrong unit for those modes.
findings.suggestion: Choose the unit with a switch on every supported load mode, for example cc→A, cp→W, cr→Ω and cv→V. You could also add a helper that returns the unit for a given mode.

finding.title: AC sweep accepts electronic loads without regard to CP mode linearization
finding.message: AC analysis now accepts `electronic-load` for both CC and CP modes. A CP load has an operating-point-dependent incremental conductance of G = −P/V². In its bounded low-voltage continuation region it behaves differently again. If the AC stamping (not visible in this part) treats the load as an ideal current sink (open circuit), CP-mode small-signal results will be silently wrong. Pulsed sources and pulsed loads also need a defined AC treatment.
finding.suggestion: Check that the AC linearization stamps the CP-mode incremental conductance at the DC operating point. If it does not, reject `electronic-load` in CP mode in `acSupported` with a clear message. Add a test covering AC with a CP load.
